# Problem 1

## Writing a function that, for a fixed group size, randomly draws “birthdays” for each person 
```{r}
sim_birthday = function(n) {
  birthday = sample(1:365, size = n, replace = TRUE)
  duplicate = length(unique(birthday)) < n
  return(duplicate)
}
```

## Running function 10000 times for each group size between 2 and 50 (computing the probability that at least two people in the group will share a birthday by averaging across the 10000 simulation runs for each group)
```{r}
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)

sim_results_df = 
  expand_grid(
    group_size = 2:50,
    iter = 1:10000
  ) |> 
  mutate(
    shared = map_lgl(group_size, sim_birthday)
  ) |> 
  group_by(group_size) |>
  summarize(
    prob_shared = mean(shared)
  )
```

## Making a plot showing the probability as a function of group size
```{r}
sim_results_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = group_size, y = prob_shared)) +
  geom_point() +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Probability that at least two people share a birthday",
    x = "Group size",
    y = "Estimated probability"
  )
```
Comment: The probability that at least two people in the group will share a birthday forms a s-shaped curved as group size increase. The value starts at around 0 when group size is small and rises quickly after the group size reaches 10. It goes above 0.5 at a group size of 23. By the group size of 50, it reaches a plateau near 1, suggesting that a shared birthday is almost certain.

# Problem 2

## Importing the datasets
```{r, message=FALSE}
study_df =
  tibble(
    name = list.files("data/", pattern = "\\.csv$")
  )

study_df =
  study_df |>
  mutate(
    data = map(str_c("data/", name), read_csv)
  )|>
  unnest(data)
```

## Tidying the datasets
```{r}
study_df =
  study_df |>
  janitor::clean_names()|>
  mutate(
    name = str_remove(name, "\\.csv$")
  ) |>
  separate(name, into = c("arm", "subject_id"), sep = "_") |>
  mutate(
    arm = case_match(
      arm,
      "con" ~ "Control",
      "exp" ~ "Experimental"
   )
  )|>
  mutate(
    subject_id = str_c(arm, "_", subject_id)
  )|>
  pivot_longer(
    cols = starts_with("week_"),
    names_to = "week",
    names_prefix = "week_",
    values_to = "observation"
  ) |>
  mutate(
    week = as.numeric(week)
  )

study_df
```

## Spaghetti plot showing observations on each subject over time
```{r}
study_df |>
  ggplot(aes(x = week, y = observation, group = subject_id, color = arm)) +
  geom_point(alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line() +
  labs(
    title = "Observations on each subject over time",
    x = "Week",
    y = "Observation",
    color = "Arm"
  )
```

Comment: Both arms start at similar observed values at week 1. As time passes, the observed values for subjects in the experimental arm demonstrate a general trend of increase. In contrast, the observed values for subjects in the control arm stays relatively unchanged. This trend suggests that the experiment is associated with an increase in the observed outcome over time.
